item.title: US court rejects Trump’s emergency order keeping Michigan coal plant open
item.description:
The Department of Energy overstepped when it ordered an aging coal-fired power plant in Michigan to stay open past its planned retirement date last year, a federal court ruled on Friday. The J.H Campbell plant is one of seven fossil fuel plants around the country that the Trump administration has forced to stay in operation, despite the pollution they cause and the enormous costs of keeping them online. Just before it was about to close last May, Trump’s Energy Department invoked short-term emergency powers under the Federal Power Act to keep the 64-year-old plant running, arguing that the threat of outages, along with the need for more energy to power data centers, constituted an emergency. But the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit rejected that argument , with Appeals Court Judge Cornelia Pillard writing that the emergency statute “is essentially a narrow, last-resort…

item.title: ‘Divine triumph’: Iran celebrates Houthis’ capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coast
item.description:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States is again fighting a major war in the Middle East. Drop Site’s Ryan Grim and Murtaza Hussain speak with Vali Nasr, professor of international affairs and Middle East studies at Johns Hopkins SAIS and a former senior adviser in the Obama administration, and Rob Malley, a senior fellow at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs, former U.S. special envoy for Iran, longtime Middle East peace negotiator, and head of the Middle East program at the International Crisis Group. The conversation covers Ansarallah’s advance in Yemen, the battle over the Strait of Hormuz, Iran and the US duel strategies of economic pressure, the future of U.S. military bases in the Gulf, the collapse of the JCPOA, Iran’s nuclear calculations, and whether Washington has learned the lessons of Iraq, Afghanistan and the broader post-9/11 wars. item.title: Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?
item.description:
Donald Trump’s new promise to give a $5,000 check to every adult American citizen if Republicans win the midterm elections may be an effort to answer a variant of an age-old riddle : Can Trump devise a policy so ill-conceived that even Trump’s intelligence is insulted? Candidates often make inducements part of their campaign pitch. One obvious peculiarity of this plan is that Trump’s party already controls both chambers of Congress. Why, then, should the bonus checks be contingent on voters giving Republicans another two-year majority? Trump has told reporters that he could distribute the loot without congressional approval. This is untrue. (It’s a facially unconstitutional infringement of Congress’s spending authority.) item.title: Jimmy Kimmel Didn't Air Talarico Interview Over Fear of FCC 'Equal Time' Threats
item.description:
For the second time this year, James Talarico, the Texas Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, appeared on a late-night talk show only to get bumped from the nightly broadcast. In each case, both the hosts and the network seemingly buckled to pressure from President Donald Trump and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). And just like in that earlier case, it provides a perfect example of why we should abolish the equal time rule. "I'll be interviewing James Talarico tomorrow night under unusual circumstances," Jimmy Kimmel said Wednesday on his ABC talk show. But the TV audience would not see the segment because of fears that by airing it, ABC's affiliates could run afoul of the equal opportunities requirement , better known as the equal time rule. item.title: The Supreme Law Without 9/11
item.description:
Today we consider the aftermath of the 25 years of U.S. foreign policy since 9/11 with a film review by Zito Madu , a journalist and author of The Minotaur at Calle Lanza . Issue No. 646 On Looking Away Zito Madu On Looking Away by Zito Madu I went to see American Doctor at the Angelika theater in Manhattan recently, a screening presented by Acacia .
